verdicts.where: Avatar: The Last Airbender's waterbenders, stronger the more water stands around them; Pokemon weather and terrain boosts; salt as the bane of slugs and the unquiet dead in folklore. The deferred Salt echoes the bends in diving thrillers, where the harm lands on leaving the water.

Grimm's Godfather Death, where every life is a candle burning down in Death's cave (retold by the Candle Maker in The Book of Life); Litwick in Pokemon, a candle ghost whose flame burns life; the lantern-bearing necromancers who raise the skeletons again in the Dark Souls catacombs. The life-candle image is stock; the wick-length and relight rules are not.

The life-as-candle of Godfather Death and 'burning the candle at both ends'; weapons that still work, poorly, below their stat requirement in Dark Souls. No story or creature has the wick-to-girth mismatch rule.

Equip load and encumbrance in Dark Souls and tabletop role-playing games; the folk-tale miser dragged under by the gold in his pockets. A price paid in depth rather than in speed is not something I can place.

Pliny's remora holding a ship fast, and the becalmed ship of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner that then lurches half her length; Red Light, Green Light in Squid Game for a crowd that halts and surges on one beat; ordinary slowing effects otherwise.

Oisin home from Tir na nOg, on whom three hundred years land the instant he touches Irish soil, and King Herla's riders who crumble on dismounting; the bends in diving stories; Bloodseeker's Rupture in Dota 2, harm that waits on the victim's own movement; marks detonated by a second skill.

'Mostly dead' against 'all dead' in The Princess Bride; downed-but-not-out windows in Gears of War and co-operative shooters, where an execution closes the window; the parlour trick of relighting a candle through its smoke.
The Swamps of Sadness in The NeverEnding Story, where whoever slows and gives in is taken by the mire, and quicksand scenes generally; chill stacking toward a freeze in Diablo and Path of Exile.

Sleeping Beauty's castle and Miss Havisham's stopped clocks, everything held exactly as it was until the spell is broken; stasis fields in science fiction (Vinge's bobbles); sleep effects that break on a hard hit; Temporal Chains in Path of Exile slowing the expiry of effects.

Nothing close. Distantly: a sheepdog turning a flock by working one flank, a matador's side-step bending the bull's line, the one-oared boat that circles in cartoons. Confusion and knockback effects in games do not hold a fixed lean set by the side struck.

Sonic's spilled rings; the leaking sack that lays a trail (Hansel and Gretel's crumbs, the cartoon burglar's swag bag); Steal and Mug in Final Fantasy and the treasure goblin of Diablo III shedding gold as it is hit, for loot taken from a living enemy.

Mayhew's mudlarks and the 1950 film The Mudlark; Dodger, Pratchett's tosher working London's sewers for finds; the scavenger-rogue archetype. Standing still for a bonus exists as an occasional item in horde games (Statue and Barricade in Brotato), not as the way to gather.

Mr. 3 (Galdino) in One Piece, whose Wax-Wax Fruit builds him a wax armour that is knocked away in the fight; Achilles dipped in the Styx; buffs that stack and fall off when hit. A lap out from and back to a vat the player places is not something I can find.

Kedging as an escape in sea stories (USS Constitution in 1812, Patrick O'Brian's novels); the mobility gear of Attack on Titan, which fires anchors and reels the soldier to them; Nautilus's Dredge Line in League of Legends; hop-only movement in Frogger. None forbids walking outright on a fixed beat.

Gaffer Hexam dragging the Thames in Dickens's Our Mutual Friend; Marley's ghost trailing his chain; the playground game crack-the-whip; physics flails whose harm is their swing speed (Hammerfight). A lagging tail that bites only on a turn is its own.

Alan Wake's torch, where a cone of light is the weapon and a boosted flash stops the Taken, and the stun flash of Luigi's Mansion; dousing your lantern so the hunters lose you in Amnesia: The Dark Descent; the bullseye and hooded lanterns of Dungeons & Dragons; the dark lantern Holmes shutters in The Red-Headed League.
verdicts.mutation: Let the light itself do no harm: each lit body throws a shadow down the cone and skills land only in those shadows, so the front rank becomes the lens that aims at the ranks behind, and the Lanternman fights by choosing whose shadow falls on whom.

verdicts.where: Jaws and the drowners of folklore (Jenny Greenteeth, the kelpie, the Inferi dragging Harry under the lake in Half-Blood Prince): an unseen thing beneath the surface pulls victims down as it passes. Walking the bottom under trapped air is Jack and Will beneath the upturned boat in Pirates of the Caribbean; going under out of sight is Pyke's Ghostwater Dive in League of Legends and Dive in Pokemon.
verdicts.mutation: Drop the drag-under: let the bell's spilled air lift whatever he walks beneath, so surface bodies bob helpless and are carried off by the surface current while he goes the other way on the undertow. He then sorts a crowd between two currents instead of playing the shark.

verdicts.where: D. M. Cornish's Monster Blood Tattoo, whose second book is Lamplighter: lamplighters walk a fixed stretch of road at dusk with a pole, lighting the lamps and fighting the monsters on it. Also the lamplighter of The Little Prince bound to his round, the street lamps that are safe havens in Alan Wake, and captured towers that fire for you.
verdicts.mutation: Have each lamp keep what he did as he passed it, not his whole kit: it repeats on a loop the exact casts made inside its pool on his last visit, so a lamp is a recording of one stretch of the round and the player composes the district by which skill fired where.

verdicts.where: Beachcombers and wreck-pickers working the strandline in shore fiction; bonus strips marked on an arena floor in games. No story or creature repeats it; the tide redrawing the line is the fresh part.

Talos, the bronze man whose making reads like lost-wax casting, and Achilles dipped in the Styx; stacks cashed into something permanent (Nasus and Veigar in League of Legends). Going bare by choice, at a place, is its own.

Gaffer Hexam, paid for the drowned he hauls from the Thames in Our Mutual Friend; Achilles dragging Hector behind his chariot; bounty hunters hauling bodies in for pay (The Hateful Eight) and resurrection men paid by the corpse; carry-and-deliver cargo in capture modes.

The wreckers' false light of Cornish legend (du Maurier's Jamaica Inn, the fire lit by the founders in Carpenter's The Fog); the flare thrown to draw the tyrannosaur in Jurassic Park and the pipe bomb in Left 4 Dead; spell totems and decoy totems in Path of Exile. The all-or-nothing split is the new part.

Haydn's Farewell Symphony, where each player snuffs his candle and leaves, and Tenebrae itself; The One (2001) and Highlander, where each rival removed makes the survivors stronger; the blinded hero whose other senses sharpen (Daredevil); thinning a deck in card roguelikes.

The carried pocket of dry air: Aang's air bubble in Avatar: The Last Airbender, the Bubble-Head Charm in Harry Potter, the parted Red Sea in small; Sonic topping up from air bubbles under water. A dry circle that changes the ground's rules and is sized by depth is in none of them.

The snowspeeder's tow cable wound round the walker's legs in The Empire Strikes Back; the dally round the saddle horn and the snubbing post of Westerns; Spider-Man's swing; tetherball. Wrapping a post to become immovable is its own.

The Red Sea standing back to leave dry ground, and firebenders flashing water to steam in Avatar; ground zones laid by skills in action games. A harmless zone that only changes which rules the ground obeys is hard to place in any story.

The bloodhound given a scrap of its quarry's scent; the witcher's blade oils, each good against one kind of monster; the ranger's favoured enemy and Hunter's Mark in Dungeons & Dragons. A mark taken by the strike and overwritten every cast is its own.

Being pixy-led, or stepping on the Irish stray sod: the walker is turned about and sent back the way he came; Turn Undead in Dungeons & Dragons; Charybdis and Poe's Maelstrom for the whirl. Eddies that exist only where the player brushes an obstacle are new to me.

The snapped cable that scythes through the ballroom in Ghost Ship (2002); the nanofilament strung across the canal in The Three-Body Problem; the harbour chain raised at the Blackwater in A Clash of Kings; tether beams between the player and a drone in games.

The magic circle that has power only when its line is closed, with Okami's brush loops and Pokemon Ranger's capture loops; the light-cycle trails of Tron, deadly to cross. A trail that fires along its whole length when its maker cuts back across it is not quite any of these.

Winnowing: the wind carries the chaff away and drops the grain at the thresher's feet; gold-panning; the rip current of sea thrillers. Separate push and pull skills are ordinary; one cast that sorts a crowd by weight is not.

Bide and Counter in Pokemon and Zed's Death Mark in League of Legends, stored harm paid back; Echo of myth, who can only repeat; flood marks cut on church walls. Replaying one record blow per toll, unscaled, is its own.

The kicked Koopa shell in Super Mario and the football in Survivor.io; furniture adrift in Titanic's flooding saloons and every flood scene. A battering object that only the tide and a shoulder can steer is its own.

Heracles turning two rivers through the Augean stables; the Ents loosing the Isen on Isengard; the flood at the Ford of Bruinen; the drained city of New Londo in Dark Souls. A channel aimed by the ground that leaves both depths changed is new.

Horatius and every held bridge; the matador stepping aside; the judo maxim of yielding so that the pusher's own force throws him; the dead heaped against the wall in World War Z. Attacks charged by standing still are ordinary; charging one with the crowd's own press is not.
The single-stroke passing duel of samurai film and anime, where two run past each other and one falls; the joust; the Road Runner's wake; graze scoring in bullet-hell shooters.

Southey's The Inchcape Rock and Kipling's The Bell Buoy for a bell the swell rings; bells that harm or bind the dead in Garth Nix's Sabriel and in church-bell folklore; drifting sea mines. A pulse that answers jostling ring for ring is its own.

The kill that forecloses what follows: exile in Magic: The Gathering and Polymorph or Silence against Deathrattles in Hearthstone (removed, so no death trigger and no return); balefire in The Wheel of Time; salt-and-burn in Supernatural; burning the bodies before they rise as Crimson Heads in Resident Evil. Culling strike supplies the threshold.
verdicts.mutation: Let the snuffer keep what it smothers: each death effect it prevents is held under the bell, and all of them are poured out together the next time it comes down on an enemy above 25%, so the player harvests the crowd's own bursts and spends them where it matters.

verdicts.where: The plate-spinner running back to each pole before it falls; the lamplighter of The Little Prince; votive candles left burning in any church scene; delayed mines in games. Ripening charges that only the player's return can spend are its own.

The reflection as a second self: Dark Link stepping out of the still pool in Ocarina of Time's Water Temple, Narcissus, the Mirror Image spell; multi-cast supports in Path of Exile. Tying the repeat to slack water is the new part.

Power that waxes and wanes on a clock: Gawain's strength growing until noon (Escanor in The Seven Deadly Sins), werewolves and the moon, waterbenders at the full moon in Avatar. No story uses the rule-of-twelfths curve itself.

Everything timed to the stroke of the bell: Cinderella's midnight, the synchronised charges of a heist film; remote mines and trap supports in Path of Exile; Zilean's time bombs in League of Legends. A store that only the run's own toll releases is its own.

The Absorbing Man of Marvel comics, who takes on the nature of whatever he touches (and Kevin Levin in Ben 10); Secret Power and Nature Power in Pokemon, one move whose effect is decided by the ground the fight stands on.
verdicts.mutation: Make it carry ground rather than copy it: the skill takes its rider from the floor under the character at the cast and delivers it only onto a victim standing on a different floor, so it does nothing on uniform ground and pays for fighting across an edge of wet and dry, silt and stone.

verdicts.where: Burning the candle at both ends; Sonic's spilled rings; Hippomenes dropping golden apples behind him in the race with Atalanta; the leaking sack that lays a trail. Speed bought by spilling your own gains into the pursuit is its own.

Facing weapons: the Knife and Whip of Vampire Survivors strike the way the character moves; Cyclops's visor and the blinkered horse; narrower-but-longer cone trade-offs in action role-playing skill trees. The same dark-lantern cone is already the Lanternman's.
verdicts.mutation: Fix the sector to the world, not the feet: the skill reaches double into one compass sector, set by where the character was heading as the toll struck and held for the whole tide like a lighthouse's sector light, so the player fights by where they stand and not by which way they run.

verdicts.where: The Borg adapting after the first phaser hit; 'the same technique never works twice on a Saint' in Saint Seiya; Doomsday, who cannot be killed the same way twice; bonuses against still-healthy enemies such as Ambush in Diablo III. Choosing that immunity as the price is its own.

Ley lines: straight alignments between landmarks (Watkins's church towers and beacons in The Old Straight Track) along which, in fantasy from The Raven Cycle to the Geomantic Web of Total War: Warhammer, power runs and magic is stronger for whoever stands on them.
verdicts.mutation: Give the line no power of its own and pay for pilotage: reach grows the longer the character keeps under way along the line with the two lights held one above the other, and falls to nothing the moment they stray or stop, so it rewards holding a bearing through the crowd, not standing on a seam of power.

verdicts.where: The Sargasso Sea of sea stories, where every drifting hulk ends up; Poohsticks; experience gems merging into one large gem in Vampire Survivors. Loot sent away to known lees and paid at a premium is its own.

The life-token of folktale (the knife that rusts when a brother is in peril in Grimm's The Two Brothers) and Meleager's brand; bonded pairs where one's death maims the other (soldier bonds in XCOM 2, dragon and rider); Link Skills in MapleStory.

Odysseus's crew with beeswax in their ears, deaf to the Sirens and to everything else; the wrapped mummy; anti-magic heroes whom healing magic cannot reach either; two-faced keystones such as Chaos Inoculation in Path of Exile.

Pokemon evolutions decided by where the creature stands when the level arrives: Eevee by the Moss Rock or the Ice Rock, Magneton in a magnetic field, Burmy's cloak taken from the ground of its last battle. The wax-in-water divination (lead-pouring, St Andrew's Eve wax) is the dressing.
verdicts.mutation: Do not pick from four named shapes: let the wax record the next three seconds of the character's own motion, with distance carried becoming reach, turning becoming area and depth becoming weight, in proportion, so every Pour is a one-off casting of that moment.

verdicts.where: The thing bared only at low water: wrecks and causeways shown by the ebb in shore tales (the Nine Lives Causeway in The Woman in Black); bonus zones in arena games. A reward line that travels with the water's edge is its own.

Running the gauntlet; the Argo shooting the Clashing Rocks; the Millennium Falcon threading the asteroid field; near-miss boost in Burnout. Stacks earned only at the map's narrows with the crowd at the shoulder are its own.

The time-locked vault and the marshmallow test; Faust's bargain turned round (pay now, collect at the appointed bell); Chaos boons in Hades and the Invisible Joker in Balatro, which pay out after a set count; interest in Teamfight Tactics.

The sacrifice of the dearest thing: Polycrates throwing his most prized ring into the sea, Agamemnon and Iphigenia, the Soul Stone's price in Avengers: Infinity War; devil deals in The Binding of Isaac and N'loth trading away a relic in Slay the Spire.
verdicts.mutation: Do not buy generic power with it: let the jettisoned find be burned for itself, its own properties coming back as in-run upgrades at double strength for this vigil only, so the player chooses to use the keepsake up now rather than carry it home.

verdicts.where: Commanding the tide and the weather: Canute's failed order, Prospero's storm, the wind-knots witches sold to sailors, the Sun's Song turning night to day in Ocarina of Time; choosing the next room's modifier in roguelikes.
Achilles held by the heel in the Styx, protected exactly as far up as the water reached; flood marks on walls; risk-for-buff choices refreshed each wave in horde games.

The floater: the bloated drowned dead of zombie fiction and games (Dead Island's Floater, the drowners of The Witcher, the Drownies of Sunless Sea), and the dead that come in with the tide (the sea-floor walkers washing ashore in World War Z, the revenants of The Fog). Hazards riding a current supply the movement.
verdicts.mutation: Keep the tide as its only legs but make it something the flood lifted, not something that drowned: a raft of wax-fused hassocks and coffin boards with a passenger aboard, which can be boarded, ridden or broken up as it passes.

verdicts.where: Corpse candles of Welsh folklore (a walking flame that foretells a death), Litwick, and the life-candles of Godfather Death; the Fallen Shaman raising the Fallen in Diablo II and the Crimson Heads of Resident Evil for the dead put down but not out. Revival by a passing flame, on a body that is burning itself away, is its own.

The lumbering dead diver in brass: BioShock's Big Daddy, Captain Cutler's ghost in Scooby-Doo; Antaeus, unbeatable only while he stands on his own ground, and the knights drowned by their armour on the ice in Alexander Nevsky. A bell on legs whose shield is squeezed off by depth is new.

The shambling bandaged Mummy crossed with a pond-skater or the basilisk lizard that runs on water; the seal and the crocodile, terrors afloat and helpless ashore. Speed and harm both read from the surface underfoot is its own.

Lot's wife, the salt vampire of Star Trek's The Man Trap, Aquaman's old weakness of dying if kept out of the water, and the Little Mermaid's knives underfoot on land. An enemy that deals nothing itself and arms the safe ground is its own.

The dead asleep in their mounds who wake when disturbed: Tolkien's barrow-wights, the Norse mound-dwellers, the draugr sitting dormant among the treasure in Skyrim's barrows; the Stalchildren that rise from Hyrule Field when night falls; the egg field of Alien. The flood plays the part of nightfall.
verdicts.mutation: Wake them by drying, not by footsteps: each mound hatches once it has lain bare for ten seconds and beds down again when covered, so a line of waking follows the ebb down the shore and the only quiet ground is the strip the water has just left.

verdicts.where: The yellow barrels that track the unseen shark in Jaws, and the dorsal fin generally; Bootstrap Bill sunk tied to a cannon and the cursed crew walking the sea bed in Pirates of the Caribbean; the wolf drowned with a belly of stones in Grimm. Striking the float to blind the walker is the part I cannot place.

The will-o'-the-wisp: jack-o'-lantern, hinkypunk, the Fenland Lantern Men, the lights in the Dead Marshes ('don't follow the lights'), the anglerfish's lure in Finding Nemo, and the wreckers' false light of Jamaica Inn. The missing reflection is the vampire's tell, and the ambush on approach is the mimic chest.

The antlion's pit and the Sarlacc, a funnel you slide into and cannot climb out of; the lobster pot; crusher-and-conveyor hazards in games. A trap that is also the district's loot collector and empties at slack water is its own.

The conveyor to the furnace in Toy Story 3 and the sawmill belt of the serials; the mine cart of Temple of Doom; trains that cross an arena on a timetable in action games. Its use as transport and crowd disposal is the fresh part.

The heap-of-bodies monster (Legion in Castlevania, The One Reborn in Bloodborne, Gravelord Nito); the wax poppet of sympathetic magic, turned round so that the wax limb takes the matching limb's power; the Black Knight losing limbs in Monty Python. Spending its own body on three readable thefts is its own.

Tenebrae itself; Zhuge Liang's seven-star lamps in Romance of the Three Kingdoms, a life staked on keeping the lamps alight; the lights put out one by one for a fight in the dark in Wait Until Dark and The Silence of the Lambs; clock-face sector attacks in raid bosses.

Talos, the bronze giant with one weak place; the bell-founding tales (Hearn's The Soul of the Great Bell, the casting in Andrei Rublev); part-breaking and wounds in Monster Hunter, where the hunter's earlier hits make the weak point. A second phase cast from the first phase's damage is its own.

The flooding chamber of adventure serials (the trash compactor, every rising-water trap); the sluice-keeper of Sayers's The Nine Tailors; the stock boss rule of sheltering behind the boss or in the storm's eye. Water level as the phase counter is the fresh part.

Hauptmann's play The Sunken Bell; the candle guttering in a sealed vault (The Cask of Amontillado) and the submarine crew dousing lights to save air; the cage match of Thunderdome and duel realms such as Mordekaiser's in League of Legends; being swallowed to strike from inside (Jonah, Jabu-Jabu).

The drowned cathedral of Ys (Debussy's La cathedrale engloutie) and New Londo in Dark Souls for the place; tilting-deck fights such as Leviathan's barge in Final Fantasy XIV for the slosh. A standing wave the player rides end to end is its own.

Old London Bridge as fiction has it; the Clashing Rocks and Charybdis, a strait that opens and reverses on a rhythm; one-way gates on a timer in arena maps. Two halves taking turns as the trap is the fresh part.

The marshes and prison hulks of Great Expectations, the tidal sands of The Riddle of the Sands, the causeway of The Woman in Black; the maze whose walls move each night in The Maze Runner; day and night map states.

Nothing close. Distantly: the canonical hours of a Book of Hours, one office to each bell in fixed order; an Advent candle burned a band a day; a step sequencer's moving light. No tree I know lets the player schedule which node is alight at which toll.

Pencil then ink, wet clay then fired pot; the choice that closes the other doors for good (the Grail knight's 'choose wisely'); free respec set against permanent ascendancy choices in Path of Exile. Half-strength trial nodes are not something I have met.

Potency thinning with distance from the source and restored where two lines join: vampire generations in Vampire: The Masquerade, the Bene Gesserit crossing of bloodlines in Dune; redstone signal fading block by block until a repeater restores it in Minecraft; travel nodes in Path of Exile.

Two natures that take turns on the world's clock: Ladyhawke, Castor and Pollux, the Oak King and the Holly King, the Summer and Winter courts; Night Stalker in Dota 2, strong by night and plain by day. Laying it out as two banks of one tree is its own.

The palimpsest and the pentimento, where older layers lie buried under the new and can be recovered; the Defect's orb slots in Slay the Spire, where a new orb pushes out an old one; affix crafting in Path of Exile. A strict last-on-first-off stack of properties is new to me.

Notches cut on a gun and kill marks on a fuselage; the named sword whose worth is its history; Strange weapons in Team Fortress 2 and legendary gems ranked by rift depth in Diablo III. A depth record replacing rarity outright is the fresh part.

The weapon written by its use: Vagrant Story, where a blade's affinities drift toward whatever it is used against; Fable III's weapons, which morph and unlock bonuses according to the wielder's deeds; skills raised by use in The Elder Scrolls; Gryffindor's sword taking in what strengthens it.
verdicts.mutation: Take an impression, not a tally: once per vigil the player presses the tablet, and the blank line is written from exactly what is true in that second (depth, current, crowd at the shoulder, life missing), so the line is a staged moment and not a season of habits.

verdicts.where: Mint in the box: Pandora's jar and Urashima's casket, Stinky Pete in Toy Story 2, sealed weapon cases in Counter-Strike and unopened booster packs, worth more shut; unidentified items in Diablo, and Path of Exile's vendor recipes paying double for unidentified sets.
verdicts.mutation: Let the seal ripen what it hides: every toll the item is worn unbroken improves the three properties inside, and a keeper's blow that breaks it early spoils them, so the question is how long to lay it down, not whether to scratch a ticket.

verdicts.where: The sea drawing back before the wave in tsunami stories (Hearn's A Living God, The Impossible); sheltering behind a pillar from the dragon's breath, and line-of-sight mechanics in raid bosses; screen-crossing hazard waves. Moving horde and loot along with the player is the fresh part.

Musical chairs, and the last-second bid at any auction scene; stand-in-the-circle shrines in action role-playing and horde games. The real auction by candle is rarely told, and its uncertain instant is the fresh part.

The vigil over the dead: Khoma keeping three nights in the church in Gogol's Viy while the candles gutter; corpse runs in Dark Souls and ZombiU, and the Shrieker returning lost trinkets in Darkest Dungeon; hold-the-point events. Winning the goods back by guarding a flame with a different character is its own.

Noah's ark lifting on the flood and grounding where the water leaves it; the Demeter driving ashore at Whitby in Dracula, and ghost ships generally; moving platforms and refuges in games. A drifting wall that stays where it grounds is the fresh part.

The storm that douses every torch and the rain that washes clean, as stock as weather gets; one shared tempo for player and horde in Crypt of the NecroDancer and in Red Light, Green Light. Putting both sides on the dead-water beat is its own.

The fog bank that rolls in off the sea with the drowned dead and a wreckers' false light in its history is John Carpenter's The Fog; also The Mist, Silent Hill, the London pea-souper, and darkness or low-visibility modifiers in any action game. Fog that shortens sight while things wait in it is stock weather under its own name.

Rogue Legacy, where Charon takes all unspent gold at the castle door, so each run's haul must pay for an upgrade by itself; the nine cities of Troy and the flood-plain record for the image of one layer per event.
verdicts.mutation: Give each layer a kind as well as a thickness, taken from how the vigil ended (in deep water, on dry stone, at a keeper, at a gate), and let nodes root only in the kind they need, so what a run can buy depends on where and how it ended and not only on how long it lasted.

verdicts.where: The mask of the dead that lends the dead one's strength: the Goron and Zora masks of Majora's Mask, the Roman wax ancestor masks, the Hall of Faces in A Song of Ice and Fire; in games, Sunless Sea's legacy handing the next captain half of one of the dead captain's stats, and Rogue Legacy's heirs.
verdicts.mutation: Make the mask a mould, not a gift: it adds nothing, but lifts any wearer who falls below half the dead one's mark in that stat up to that floor and drops away once they outgrow it, so the dead shore up what the living lack.

verdicts.where: Flood marks and records made to be broken; level select and continue-from-wave in arcade games (Tempest), rifts opened up to the highest cleared in Diablo III, heat records in Hades. Choosing the skipped picks in a row is the fresh part.

The plot run by the tide table (The Riddle of the Sands, the causeway of The Woman in Black); Salmon Run in Splatoon, a horde mode whose waves come at high or low tide; wave timers generally. A readable twelfths curve inside every interval is its own.

The door that opens only at the appointed moment and place (Durin's Day in The Hobbit, causeways passable at low water); in games, Exfil in Call of Duty Zombies, offered every few rounds at a fixed site as the rounds step up, and the camp tile in Loop Hero, where each lap asks whether to bank or go round again harder.
verdicts.mutation: Hold to the physical rule and let the player use it: any gate opens the moment the water stands level on both sides, so the toll gives one opening per tide, but a character who can level water elsewhere (a sluice, a pan, a grounded hulk) can make a way out off the clock.

verdicts.where: Magic that runs out at the bell (Cinderella) and gains that fade in turn (Flowers for Algernon); Perishable jokers in Balatro and food that spoils in Don't Starve; boons that last a set number of rooms in Hades. Every upgrade on one clock, in the order taken, is the fresh part.

Buried treasure left for the heir: Treasure Island, Faria's hoard passed to Dantes in The Count of Monte Cristo; in games, NetHack's bones files, the stash a new survivor reclaims in Project Zomboid, buried stashes in DayZ, and the bloodstain of Dark Souls.
verdicts.mutation: Let the water work on what is left in its keeping: each vigil a find lies sunk rewrites one of its properties after that district's kind (a sea-change), so lagan is a slow craft and the question is when to raise it, not only whether it is safe.

verdicts.where: The run that is made real when it succeeds: Pinocchio, and the apprentice's masterpiece; in games, Wildermyth promoting a finished campaign's heroes into the legacy roster, and league characters migrating to Standard in Path of Exile and Diablo, one way only.
verdicts.mutation: Cast the other layer: what the pour keeps is the run's set of in-run upgrades, frozen as the standing character's fixed innate kit, while levels and worn items are what melt away, so each standing character is the lasting shape of one whole run.

verdicts.where: The thief dragged down by his own loot (The Treasure of the Sierra Madre, the Cave of Wonders); cargo and ballast thrown out to stay up, as in the balloon that opens Verne's The Mysterious Island; Gil Toss in Final Fantasy, money thrown for harm equal to its worth; encumbrance. Weight as steadiness against the water is the fresh part.

Curse of the Dead Gods, where every offering can be paid for in gold or taken free at the cost of creeping corruption; Darkest Dungeon's torch, light traded against reward; the quick and easy path of the dark side. Tallow against beeswax is true social history, rarely told.
verdicts.mutation: Tie the smoke to the casting, not the owning: each tallow skill dims the character's light for two seconds every time it fires, so the dark flickers on the build's own rhythm and can be read and played in the gaps, and beeswax buys silence in that rhythm.

verdicts.where: Watertight doors and flooding compartments in Titanic and submarine films; the dead pressed against the mall doors in Dawn of the Dead; arenas with gates on a timer. Doors worked by their own swelling, each opening levelling two rooms, is its own.

Swimming a witch (the guilty float); the nail-weighted candle that rides higher as it burns; low-life builds in Path of Exile and berserker thresholds. Missing life changing how the water treats the body is the fresh part.
